title: AI-written messages: judge the ask, not the prose
body_md:
## Read the ask, not the prose

A message lands on a Monday morning, warm, tidy, a shade too well put together, and you catch yourself hunting for the tell: would a real person write “I hope this finds you well”? The hunt feels like diligence. It is closer to a doorman who studies each visitor’s accent and never opens the guest list. He will wave in a good many liars and turn away a few honest people.

A polished message may come from a person, a translation tool, an AI editor or a template, and a clumsy one can still be fraud. No dependable rule says that AI text sounds formal, or that a real friend will always bring up a private memory. Attackers can feed a generator public details and stolen ones; a real friend can write briefly, vaguely or in a hurry. So ask the question that has an answer: **what does this message want me to do, and how can I check that outside the message?**

### Start with the action

Look at what is being asked: a new payment destination, gift cards, a login link, a one-time code, secrecy, a rush. A break from the person’s usual manner is a reason to check, not a verdict. Say an old friend mentions the new job you announced in public, then asks for a transfer. Knowing about the job proves nothing; it was never secret. A colleague who runs a request through an AI tool and asks you to open a ticket in the system you both already use is no fraudster, however smooth the wording.

### Why a memory question is not enough

Asking about a shared memory can slow an impostor down, but an independent callback is stronger. The answer may be online, sitting in a hijacked mailbox, or simply guessed. And if you reply in the same compromised thread, you leave the conversation in the attacker’s hands. Open a saved contact or the service itself. For a company invoice, compare it with the supplier record and follow the procedure for changing payment details.

### What a detector can and cannot tell you

An AI-text detector answers a narrow statistical question, under the conditions it was tested in. In NIST’s published text pilot, results varied substantially with the generator and the detector, and it tested summaries, not your friend’s email. A score cannot settle who wrote a message, let alone whether the payment it asks for is legitimate. Do not paste a private message into an outside detector for the sake of a number; you would be handing it to a stranger. If you cannot verify an urgent request, pause it. A genuine sender can usually wait while you reach them by a route you choose.

What deserves your attention is a request with consequences and no independent confirmation behind it, however good the grammar.

widget_config.goal: Judge an unexpected message by what it asks for and how you can confirm it elsewhere, without treating AI-sounding prose as proof.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one person you trust and check that you hold a saved number or address for them: the one you would use if a message from them ever asked for money or an account code.
widget_config.scope: General guidance on judging messages, checked 20 October 2026. The NIST findings come from one benchmark of text summaries and say nothing general about sorting real email. The people and cases here are invented.

sources.title: NIST: 2024 GenAI text-to-text pilot
sources.scope: Published June 2025. A benchmark built on machine-written and human-written summaries, where detector results varied from system to system. It does not show that a detector can be trusted on one individual message.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, page dated September 2023: voice cloning, urgency, calling back on a number you know, and checking with another relative. The reporting route it gives applies only in the US.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance on requests to transfer money or change account details: confirm through a second channel, and contact your bank at once if you suspect a transfer went to a fraudster. Company and national procedures differ.

blocks.title: A warm note from an old friend, and a request
blocks.situation: A message congratulates you on the new job you announced in public, mentions the town that shows up in your old posts, and then asks for an urgent transfer to a new account.
blocks.analysis: Details that feel personal can have public sources, and elegant prose proves nothing. Do not answer in the thread with a trivia test. Reach the friend on the address or number you already have, and confirm exactly what is being asked before you pay anything.

blocks.title: A stiff message from a real coworker
blocks.situation: A colleague has put their text through a translation tool and writes, “I am reaching out regarding the matter.” They want you to read an incident that is already filed in your normal work system.
blocks.analysis: Formal wording is no evidence of a scam or of AI authorship. Open the system yourself, read the incident, and answer through its usual workflow. Keep the private note away from any detector.

blocks.title: An invitation without a single typo
blocks.setup: An invented scene: a community organiser you know sends a polished message about an event and asks you to pay a new registration fee. You have never heard of this fee. Each decision is a separate snapshot; nothing you do in one carries into the next.

steps.prompt: Before you form any view of the tone, what do you pin down?

choices.text: The new fee and where the money would go
choices.consequence: You have found the part of the message that has consequences.
choices.explanation: Payment details need checking, however the message is written.

choices.text: Whether the opening paragraph sounds like AI
choices.consequence: You come away with a hunch, and the payment question is still open.
choices.explanation: A person and a generator can write in the same register.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: the message links to a page for the fee. Where do you go to check?

choices.text: Follow the link; the address looks tidy
choices.consequence: You are still walking the route the sender laid out for you.

choices.text: Open the organiser’s known site or saved contact yourself
choices.consequence: You compare the message with a source it does not control.
choices.explanation: A link supplied by the message may lead to a page an attacker built.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you open the organiser’s known site yourself and find no mention of a fee. The organiser cannot be reached. What do you do?

choices.text: Upload the message to an AI detector, and pay if it reports a low AI-likelihood score
choices.consequence: In this snapshot the detector reports a low AI-likelihood score. You have shown a private message to an outside service and paid a fee nobody confirmed.
choices.explanation: A low AI score says nothing about whether this payment is authorised.

choices.text: Hold the payment and ask later through the known route
choices.explanation: An unconfirmed fee stays unconfirmed, however polished the message that asks for it.

blocks.debrief: The safe decision was about the new fee, not about whether an AI helped write the invitation. A genuine organiser may well use a writing assistant. Go back and take the other choices to compare where they lead.

blocks.title: A fresh message, the same method

questions.prompt: An AI detector labels a private email “human”. Does that clear you to pay?

choices.text: Yes; a “human” result authenticates the sender
choices.explanation: A message written by a human can still be fraudulent, or sent from a hijacked account.

choices.text: No; verify the payment request through a route you choose
choices.explanation: Who wrote the words and who may order a payment are different questions.

questions.prompt: A genuine colleague uses a writing assistant. What does their formal prose tell you?

choices.text: Very little about whether the request is safe
choices.explanation: Look at the action being asked for, in the system you normally use.

choices.text: That the colleague must be an impostor
choices.explanation: How someone writes is not an identity test.

questions.prompt: In the suspicious thread, the sender correctly answers a question about your shared past. What follows?

choices.text: For a high-risk request, still contact them by a route you chose
choices.explanation: An attacker may have researched that history, or read it in a hijacked mailbox, and may control the thread.

choices.text: The answer on its own settles who it is
choices.explanation: Knowing a fact is not proof of control or of authority.
